Epic Fail
EP-ik FAYL
noun / interjection (Millennial slang)
The noun-interjection fail traces to the broken English of a 1998 Japanese arcade game, Blazing Star, whose game-over screen read "You fail it! Your skill is not enough." Imageboards around 2003 seized it, and "FAIL" stamped over a photo became a meme. Epic fail followed by about 2005, and in 2008 the humour site FAIL Blog (later part of Cheezburger) turned it into an industry of captioned disasters: the misspelled tattoo, the truck wedged under the bridge, the skateboarder meeting the railing. It was a Millennial staple through the early 2010s, now largely displaced by video compilations.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

An epic fail is a spectacular, public, usually funny failure, captured and shared: the botched backflip, the wedding cake on the floor, the sign that says the opposite of what it meant. The phrase is also turned on oneself ("epic fail on my part") as a light way to own a mistake. The Christian observation has two edges. First, there is a grace in being able to laugh at our own blunders; pride cannot do it, and humility can. Second, there is no grace in a culture that harvests other people’s humiliation for entertainment. "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished" (Pro 17:5). "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth" (Pro 24:17); if not over an enemy, how much less over a stranger whose worst moment went viral. And the gospel speaks a stranger word over failure itself: "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Pro 24:16). The Church is full of epic fails: Peter’s denial, Jonah’s flight, David’s rooftop. Their stories are told not as comedy but as mercy, because the Lord restores. A father tells his son: when you fail in front of everyone, own it, laugh if it is funny, and get up; and never make another man’s fall your entertainment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial slang (from a 1998 game’s "You fail it," 2003 meme, 2008 FAIL Blog) for a spectacular public failure; fine as self-mockery, wrong as entertainment harvested from another’s humiliation (Pro 17:5).

EPIC FAIL, n. / interj. (Millennial slang, c. 2005–2015) A spectacular, usually public and comic failure; also said as a verdict: "Epic fail." Short form: fail ("FAIL," "#fail").

Genre: FAIL Blog (2008), fail compilations, captioned photos of botched signs, stunts, and repairs.

Webster (1828), root fail: FAIL, verb intransitive [Latin fallo; Gr. whence; Eng. felony. It seems to be allied to fall, fallow, pale, and many other words.] 1. To become deficient; to be insufficient; to cease to be abundant for supply; or to be entirely wanting. We say, in a dry season, the springs and streams fail or are failing, before they are entirely exhausted. We say also, the springs failed, when they entirely ceased to flow. Crops fail wholly or partially. 2. To decay; to decline; to sink; to be diminished. […]

Decode for parents: the joke trains children to laugh at strangers’ worst moments; teach them to laugh at their own and to help others up.

Key Scripture

Pro 17:5 — "Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: and he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished."

Pro 24:17 — "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth:"

Pro 24:16 — "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief."

Mic 7:8 — "Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me."

Gal 6:1 — "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted."

Modern Corruption

Epic fail turns another person’s humiliation into content; Scripture forbids gladness at calamity and answers failure with restoration.

expand to see more

The corruption is the spectator’s seat. The FAIL genre runs on strangers who never consented to be laughed at by millions, and it trains the viewer to meet a fall with a smirk instead of a hand. Scripture calls that posture dangerous to the one who holds it: he that is glad at calamities "shall not be unpunished" (Pro 17:5). The mocker also forgets his own turn is coming; the man who laughs loudest at the fail video has his own recorded on some phone he never noticed.

The biblical recovery is a theology of getting up. "Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me" (Mic 7:8). Failure is not the end of a believer’s story, and the brother who sees it has a job: "if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted" (Gal 6:1). Raise children who can laugh at their own spilled milk, who refuse to forward a stranger’s humiliation, and who know that the Lord who restored Peter on the shore restores His people still.
